A Professor of AI and Applications, Prof. Abejide Ade-Ibijola, has urged governments to deploy artificial intelligence-powered solutions to improve agricultural productivity and healthcare delivery in rural communities, particularly through mobile applications and indigenous language technology. Ade-Ibijola, made the call on Saturday during an interaction with journalists in Ado Ekiti, Ekiti State, where he advocated technology-driven interventions tailored to the needs of local populations. He said AI should not be restricted to urban centres and educated technology enthusiasts but extended to rural communities where access to modern infrastructure and professional services remained limited. According to him, AI applications could help farmers predict weather conditions, improve agricultural yields and access relevant farming information, while providing rural residents with easier access to basic healthcare guidance. He said, “AI can help farmers predict weather conditions, improve agricultural yields and access relevant farming information and as well provide rural residents with easier access to basic healthcare guidance through mobile technology”. He said he was particularly interested in contributing to the development of Ekiti, his home state, and grooming young people who could sustain technology-driven initiatives beyond the tenure of any administration. Ade-Ibijola said the state’s peculiar demographic and geographical realities required an inclusive approach to AI adoption, adding that residents did not necessarily need formal technology education to benefit from its applications. He said, “We don’t have to educate residents necessarily about technology. We just have to develop technology that helps them. Such applications can provide farmers with information on weather patterns, support agricultural decision-making and help improve productivity, while similar tools could assist residents in accessing healthcare information”. On making AI accessible to rural populations, the professor identified language as a major consideration, advocating the development of machine learning and language models capable of communicating in Nigerian languages and dialects. He said, “We can develop machine learning models, language models, and they can speak in Yoruba, they can speak in Ekiti. Rural residents will find it easier to interact with technology if they can communicate with AI applications in their indigenous languages rather than being compelled to use English.” He proposed collecting and recording thousands of audio samples from native speakers of the Ekiti dialect, which could be transcribed and used to train artificial intelligence models. According to him, the initiative would enable residents to make enquiries, seek information and obtain responses through simple voice interactions on their mobile phones. Ade-Ibijola also called for stronger collaboration between governments, private-sector operators, technology companies and other stakeholders to develop and deploy AI solutions capable of addressing the state’s development challenges. He urged the state government to expose young technology entrepreneurs to international opportunities and established technology companies, including Microsoft and Huawei. He said, “The state must create an environment where young people can develop technology products, establish startup companies, generate employment and attract investment”. Abiodun Nejo
